rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Gases have two principal specific heats: C_v at constant volume and C_p at constant pressure. For ideal gases, C_p − C_v = R (Mayer's relation). The ratio γ = C_p/C_v depends on molecular degrees of freedom: monatomic γ = 5/3, diatomic γ = 7/5. These values govern adiabatic processes, sound speed, and thermodynamic cycles.

rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
Mayer's relation: $C_p - C_v = R$
Adiabatic index: $\gamma = \frac{C_p}{C_v}$
Monatomic: $C_v = \frac{3}{2}R$, $C_p = \frac{5}{2}R$, $\gamma = \frac{5}{3}$

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: Ideal Gas Assumption: Mayer's relation C_p − C_v = R holds exactly only for ideal gases. Real gases show deviations at high P or low T.  ·  Temperature Range Matters: Degrees of freedom activated depend on T. Room-temperature diatomic values assume rotation active but vibration frozen.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: Statement 1: Molar heat capacity at constant pressure exceeds that at constant volume by the gas constant R.  ·  Statement 2: The ratio γ = C_p/C_v is always greater than unity for any gas.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: Argon (monatomic): C_v = 12.47 J/(mol·K), C_p = 20.79 J/(mol·K), γ = 1.67. Difference = 8.32 ≈ R.  ·  Nitrogen at 300 K: C_v = 20.8 J/(mol·K) ≈ 5R/2, C_p = 29.1 J/(mol·K) ≈ 7R/2, γ = 1.40.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: Thinking C_p and C_v are material constants independent of process: They are defined FOR specific processes (constant P or V).  ·  Using R without checking molar vs mass basis: Molar uses R = 8.314; specific uses R/M.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: Specific Heat Definition: Amount of heat required to raise temperature of unit mass by 1 K. For gases, value depends on process conditions because gases expand significantly when heated.  ·  C_v (Constant Volume): Heat added increases only internal energy (no work done since dV = 0). Q = nC_vΔT = ΔU. For monatomic ideal gas: C_v = (3/2)R. Diatomic at room T: C_v = (5/2)R.

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: C_p − C_v = R: memorize as 'difference equals gas constant'.  ·  γ = 1 + 2/f: quick formula from DOF count.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: Q1. Derive Mayer's relation C_p − C_v = R for an ideal gas.  ·  Q2. Why is C_p always greater than C_v? Explain physically.

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: Derive Mayer's relation starting from first law and ideal gas equation.  ·  Calculate γ from experimental C_p and C_v data.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: C_p > C_v because constant-pressure heating includes expansion work.  ·  Mayer's relation: C_p − C_v = R for ideal gases.  ·  γ = C_p/C_v determines adiabatic behavior and sound speed.  ·  Degrees of freedom dictate heat capacity values via equipartition.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Julius Robert von Mayer first stated C_p − C_v = R in 1841, contributing to energy conservation principle.  ·  Einstein and Debye models explain low-temperature heat capacity anomalies using quantum statistics.

rows.label: More practice
rows.text: Q3. Calculate γ for a triatomic gas with all vibrational modes active.  ·  Q4. How does heat capacity of hydrogen change from 50 K to 3000 K?  ·  Q5. Given C_v = 20.8 J/(mol·K) for a gas, find C_p and γ.

rows.label: More hints
rows.text: Explain why C_p > C_v physically using work argument.  ·  Relate changes in γ to molecular complexity and temperature effects.

rows.label: Extra solved
rows.text: Speed of sound in air at 20°C: v = √(1.4 × 8.314 × 293 / 0.029) ≈ 343 m/s.  ·  Adiabatic compression: Air compressed from 1 atm to 8 atm. T₂/T₁ = (P₂/P₁)^((γ−1)/γ) = 8^(0.286) ≈ 1.81. If T₁ = 300 K, T₂ ≈ 543 K.

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: C_p (Constant Pressure): Heat added increases internal energy AND does expansion work against external pressure. Q = nC_pΔT = ΔU + PΔV. Always C_p > C_v because extra energy goes into work.  ·  Mayer's Relation: C_p − C_v = R for one mole of ideal gas. Derived from H = U + PV and ideal gas law. Per unit mass: c_p − c_v = R/M where M is molar mass.  ·  Adiabatic Index γ: γ = C_p/C_v. Monatomic: γ = 5/3 ≈ 1.67. Diatomic (room T): γ = 7/5 = 1.40. Polyatomic: γ ≈ 1.33. Determines adiabatic process behavior: PV^γ = constant.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Diatomic (room T): $C_v = \frac{5}{2}R$, $C_p = \frac{7}{2}R$, $\gamma = \frac{7}{5}$  ·  General: $C_v = \frac{f}{2}R$, $C_p = \left(\frac{f}{2}+1\right)R$  ·  Speed of sound: $v = \sqrt{\frac{\gamma RT}{M}}$

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Per Mole vs Per Mass: Molar heat capacities use R; specific (mass-based) use R/M. Always check units in problems.  ·  Quasi-static Processes: Definitions assume reversible, quasi-static heating. Rapid non-equilibrium heating gives different effective heat capacities.  ·  Monatomic γ = 5/3; diatomic γ = 7/5 at ordinary temperatures.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Vibrational modes increase C_v at high temperatures.  ·  Assuming γ is always 1.4: Only true for diatomic gases near room temperature. Monatomic and polyatomic differ.  ·  Believing vibrational modes always contribute: They activate only above characteristic temperatures (e.g., ~2000 K for N₂).

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Confusing heat capacity with thermal conductivity: Heat capacity stores energy; conductivity transfers it. Different physical quantities.  ·  For air (mostly N₂ + O₂), γ ≈ 1.40 at STP — matches diatomic prediction.  ·  Steam (H₂O, polyatomic) has γ ≈ 1.33; helium (monatomic) has γ ≈ 1.67.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: At cryogenic temperatures, H₂ behaves as monatomic (rotation frozen): γ → 5/3.  ·  NEB frequently asks derivation of C_p − C_v = R and calculation of γ for given molecular types.  ·  Statement 3: Heat capacity values reflect the number of active molecular degrees of freedom.
